Every number is the lesson page's own: the survey is its A4 (Walk 9, Bus 6, Car 4, Bike 3) and B4 (5, 11, 4, 2), both 22; the Venn numbers 12, 8, 15 and 7 are the four it names in its own explainer; the spinner is its four equal parts spun 10 and 1000 times.
title: Asking, Sorting and Chance
subtitle: Grade 4 Mathematics
objectives: Plan and conduct an investigation to answer statistical questions, considering what data to collect (categorical and discrete data).

Record, organise and represent categorical and discrete data. Choose and explain which representation to use in a given situation: Venn and Carroll diagrams tally charts and frequency tables pictograms and bar charts dot plots (one dot per count).
Interpret data, identifying similarities and variations, within and between data sets, to answer statistical questions. Discuss conclusions, considering the sources of variation.
Use language associated with chance to describe familiar events, including reference to maybe, likely, certain, impossible.
Conduct chance experiments, using small and large numbers of trials, and present and describe the results using the language of probability.

beats.say: How does your class get to school? Ask them all, and you have data.
Today you will record it, draw it, sort it, and say how likely it is.
First decide what would answer it. Some answers are names, some are numbers.
Walk, bus, car or bike are groups you can name. Categorical data.
How many brothers and sisters? Those are numbers you count. Discrete data.
Twenty-two children answer, one stroke each. Every fifth stroke crosses four, like a gate.
Now count in fives. Nine walk, six by bus, four by car, three by bike. Twenty-two.
The same twenty-two answers, drawn three ways. Each is good at a different job.
A bar chart gives each group a bar against a scale. Walking is tallest, at nine.
A pictogram uses a key. One circle stands for two children, so nine is four and a half.
A dot plot puts one dot for each child, so you can count them one by one.
A Venn diagram asks two questions at once. Is it even? Is it more than ten?
Twelve is even and more than ten. Both answers are yes, so it goes in the overlap.
Eight is even, but not more than ten. Fifteen is more than ten, but not even.
Seven is neither, so it sits outside both hoops. A Carroll diagram gives it its own box.
Class 4A and class 4B answered the same question. Both have twenty-two children.
In 4A walking wins, with nine. In 4B the bus wins, with eleven.
Four children come by car in each class. That is the same in both.
The same total does not mean the same answers. Look at every group.

at.notsame: does not mean the same answers

beats.say: Some things cannot happen. Some are sure to. Most sit in between.
A dice has no seven, so rolling one is impossible.
But every face is less than seven, so that is certain.

at.everyface: every face is less than seven

beats.say: A bag holds nine red counters and one blue. Red is likely, blue is unlikely.
Tossing a coin is maybe. It might land on heads, and it might not.

scenes.heading: Spin it, and spin it again

beats.say: This spinner has four equal parts, so each should come up a quarter of the time.
Ten spins are lumpy. One part came up five times, when it should be two and a half.
Now spin it a thousand times. Each part lands close to two hundred and fifty.

at.closeto: close to two hundred and fifty

beats.say: A few spins tell you little. Many spins show what the spinner really does.
You can plan what to collect, and tally it as the answers come.
You can draw it three ways, sort it two ways, and compare two classes.
And you can say if something is impossible, maybe, likely or certain. Well done.
